name: Gamay

lines.s10: Gamay is the grape of Beaujolais: a light, juicy red of sour cherry, raspberry and violet that takes a light chill well.
lines.s20: Gamay is the red grape of Beaujolais, light in colour and body and bright with acidity. It tastes of sour cherry, raspberry and violet, and the ten villages called crus make a deeper wine with a stony edge.
lines.s45: Gamay was banished from the heart of Burgundy in 1395, and it found its home to the south, on the granite hills of Beaujolais. It is light and bright, with sour cherry, raspberry and violet, high acidity and hardly any tannin. Most of it ferments as whole bunches in a sealed vat, which keeps the fruit fresh and can add a hint of banana. Oregon and Ontario tend to make it a little darker and rounder. Pour it lightly chilled with charcuterie, roast chicken or the holiday turkey. Its first wine of the year, Beaujolais Nouveau, goes on sale on the third Thursday of November.
lines.sale: Gamay is the red you can chill: all sour cherry and raspberry, with barely any tannin to turn hard in the cold. I would open it with the charcuterie, or pour it right through a table of roast chicken.

glass.lead: Sour cherry, raspberry and cranberry with violet and peony, light and juicy, on high acidity and very little tannin.

ladder.where: Beaujolais, Touraine, the Niagara Peninsula and the Willamette Valley
The sunny Swiss Valais, and the granite crus in a warm year

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, tannin low, alcohol moderate, body light, rising to medium in the crus.

old.where: Beaujolais and its ten crus; Touraine in the Loire; the Swiss Valais
old.glass: Tends to be light and tart: sour cherry, raspberry and violet, often with the banana and bubblegum of whole bunch fermentation in the simpler wines, and crushed granite and more grip in the crus.
old.cellar: Mostly whole bunches in a sealed vat, the semi-carbonic way, pressed early; the crus are increasingly destemmed and aged in old casks, like red Burgundy.

new.where: Oregon's Willamette Valley and Ontario's Niagara Peninsula
new.glass: Typically a shade darker and rounder: red cherry, black cherry and cranberry over freshly turned soil, with bright acidity and soft tannin. The candied banana note is less common.
new.cellar: Often made as Pinot Noir is, destemmed or partly whole bunch and rested in old barrels; some growers use whole bunches in the Beaujolais manner.

contrast.why: Beaujolais built its style on whole bunch fermentation and early bottling, on granite. Growers in Oregon and Ontario often came to Gamay through Pinot Noir and use its cellar. The French label names a village, the New World the grape.
contrast.blur: The serious crus, Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent above all, are now often made like red Burgundy, and some Oregon and Ontario growers make a carbonic or Nouveau style.
contrast.call: Banana, violet and crushed granite on a light, tart frame lean Beaujolais; darker cherry, rounder fruit and no candied note lean Oregon or Ontario.

service.temp: 54 to 59 degrees Fahrenheit, 12 to 15 degrees Celsius; Nouveau a little cooler still.
service.glass: A Burgundy bowl for a cru; a plain red wine glass serves a simple Beaujolais.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary. A young, firm Morgon may open with a little air.
service.age: Young, within two or three years; a cru such as Morgon or Moulin-à-Vent keeps ten.

with.why: high acidity cuts the fat, as in the bistros of Lyon
a light red that does not crowd the bird
tart cherry fruit echoes the sauce
served cool, with little tannin to clash with smoke and pepper

labels.means: The middle tier, from the granite hamlets of the north: riper and firmer than plain Beaujolais.
Three of the ten crus: the label names the village and need not say Beaujolais or Gamay.
The first wine of the harvest, released on the third Thursday of November and drunk young.
A name on Oregon and Ontario labels; in full Gamay Noir à Jus Blanc, black skinned with white juice.
An old California name for a clone of Pinot Noir, not true Gamay; barred from American labels since 2007.

guest.a: No. Nouveau is the first and simplest wine of the year. A cru such as Morgon or Moulin-à-Vent is a serious red that can keep ten years and grow to taste like Burgundy.
In law it belongs to greater Burgundy, but it is its own country: Gamay on granite, not Pinot Noir on limestone, and a lighter, juicier wine.

guest.q: Can you really chill a red wine?
guest.a: This one, yes. Gamay has so little tannin that a light chill only lifts its fruit. A firm, tannic red would turn hard, which is why those are served warmer.

compare.tell: Pinot Noir is silkier, with forest floor beneath the fruit and a longer finish; Gamay is lighter, tarter and more candied, with a violet rim.
Loire Cabernet Franc is leafier, with green bell pepper, pencil shavings and firmer tannin; Gamay is softer and fruitier, with no green edge.
Zweigelt is darker in colour, with a peppery snap and a little more tannin; Gamay is paler and lighter, with a scent of violet.

cards.front: Gamay: where is it at home, and on what soil?
cards.back: Beaujolais, south of Burgundy, on the pink granite and schist of the northern hills, where the ten crus lie. A ducal edict of 1395 drove it out of the Côte d'Or.

cards.front: Gamay blind: Beaujolais or the New World, what tips it?
cards.back: Banana, violet and crushed granite on a light, tart frame lean Beaujolais. Darker cherry, rounder fruit and no candied note lean Oregon or Ontario, where it is often made as Pinot Noir is.

cards.front: Name the ten crus of Beaujolais, Gamay's home, north to south.
cards.back: Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Côte de Brouilly, Brouilly.

questions.q: A blind red is bright purple with a violet rim, light and tart, with sour cherry, banana and bubblegum, high acidity and almost no tannin. The table agrees it is Gamay. Which origin fits it?
questions.exp: Banana and bubblegum are the mark of carbonic maceration, the classic method of Beaujolais. Oregon and Ontario often make Gamay as they make Pinot Noir, so the candied note is less common there.

questions.q: A guest wants a bottle from Gamay's home to lay down for several years, not one to drink this month. Which label do you bring?
questions.exp: Moulin-à-Vent is a firm, structured cru that can keep ten years. Nouveau is made to drink within months, Villages is a young bistro red, and Beaujolais Blanc is Chardonnay.

questions.q: On a hot evening a guest asks for a red he can drink cool with a plate of charcuterie. Which grape do you suggest?
questions.exp: Gamay has high acidity and very little tannin, so a light chill lifts its fruit. Cabernet Sauvignon, Nebbiolo and Tannat are tannic reds that turn hard and bitter when served cold.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it, though TASTE.world reads old: the New World side is two places only, Oregon and Ontario, and is written modestly. A reviewer may prefer home and abroad; the content would carry over.

The ladder keeps Beaujolais on the cool rung, as the Court's grid reads it. The moderate rung is the Swiss Valais, which the Codex's own Switzerland reading calls dry, sunny and foehn swept, and the granite crus in a warm year. Gamay has no warm home.

The New World glass stands on the Ontario wine authority's sheet (fresh, fruity, high acidity, soft tannin), on Wine Country Ontario's signature varieties page (fruity, floral and earthy) and on a trade magazine of the American north west for Oregon (mostly made as Pinot Noir is made, some Nouveau style). No Oregon Wine Board page on Gamay was found.
Black pepper, often said of Ontario Gamay, is left out of the New World glass for want of a second source; the Codex's own profile gives a light pepper to the crus.

The label entry Gamay Beaujolais stands on the federal rule: the name was phased out and barred from labels of wine bottled from April 2007. Napa Gamay, the old name of Valdiguié, is left out to save room.
Sierra Foothills, California is a wrong option in the worlds question and nothing more is claimed for it.
The edict of 1395, the third Thursday of November, the ten crus in order and Beaujolais in law a part of greater Burgundy are the Codex's own reviewed facts (the Beaujolais reading).
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the sites directly. The VQA Ontario address is as the search returned it and should be opened by the checker.

checked.verdict: Sound after eight fixes. The edict of 1395, the ten crus in order, Nouveau, the Gamay Beaujolais rule of 2007 and the service figures hold; the New World side made Oregon and Ontario Gamay a Pinot Noir in all but name, against the Codex Oregon record, and forest floor stood among the notes though both entries and the reviewed profile part Pinot Noir from Gamay by it.
changed: glass.notes: the earth group of potting soil and forest floor is struck. Forest floor is the note the Pinot Noir tell, this entry own tell and the reviewed confuse line give to Pinot Noir and not to Gamay; potting soil stands in the New World glass as freshly turned soil.

lines.s45: a little darker and firmer now reads a little darker and rounder, as the New World glass and the Ontario sheet (soft tannin) have it, and the claim that both make it as they make Pinot Noir leaves the spoken line.

worlds.contrast.new.cellar: usually made as Pinot Noir is now reads often made as Pinot Noir is, with some growers using whole bunches in the Beaujolais manner. The Codex Oregon record calls its Gamay bright, crunchy and in the Beaujolais manner.
worlds.contrast.why: Oregon and Ontario came to Gamay through Pinot Noir now reads growers there often did; the label clause trimmed to keep the cap.
cards[1] and questions[0].exp: mostly made as Pinot Noir is now reads often, for the same reason.
labels, Gamay Noir: the name on Oregon and Ontario labels now reads a name: many print Gamay alone.
compare, the Zweigelt tell: with sour cherry is struck, since Gamay carries sour cherry too; colour, pepper and tannin part the two.
open: How much Oregon and Ontario Gamay is made whole bunch and how much destemmed: no count was found. The entry hedges both ways.
Black pepper, often said of Ontario Gamay, stays out for want of a second source, as the author left it.
